q-2770.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14187261/assets/cc27a817900f1e7bef61f73da6bbdb3aaae4e30d59490dce4395416d98f4edae.png)

The sides of a square increase in length at a rate of $2\text{ m/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square increasing when the sides are $10\text{ m}$ long?
q-2770.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of $2\,\text{m/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2.$ Also, when the sides are $10\,\text{m},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(2)\cdot 2(10)=40{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square increases at $40\,{\text{m}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

Question 1
?

The sides of a square increase in length at a rate of 2 m/s. At what rate is the area of the square increasing when the sides are 10 m long?

a
20 m/s
b
30 m2/s
c
40 m2/s
d
40 m/s
e
20 m2/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let x and A be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

dAdt.

The area A is related to side length x by the formula

A=x2.

Differentiating this relationship with respect to t using implicit differentiation, we get

ddt(A)=ddt(x2)dAdt=dxdt⋅ddx(x2)dAdt=dxdt⋅2x

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of 2m/s, so we have dxdt=2. Also, when the sides are 10m, we have x=10. Substituting this information into the above, we get

dAdt=(2)⋅2(10)=40 m2/s.

Therefore, the area of the square increases at 40m2/s.

q-73309.html:
Question 5
?

The sides of a square increase in length at a rate of 7mm/s. At what rate is the area of the square increasing when the sides are 12mm long?

a
108m2/s
b
100cm2/s
c
128mm2/s
d
168mm2/s
e
98mm2/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let x and A be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

dAdt.

The area A is related to side length x by the formula

A=x2.

Differentiating this relationship with respect to t using implicit differentiation, we get

ddt(A)=ddt(x2)dAdt=dxdt⋅ddx(x2)dAdt=dxdt⋅2x

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of 7mm/s, so we have dxdt=7. Also, when the sides are 12mm, we have x=12. Substituting this information into the above, we get

dAdt=(7)⋅2(12)=168 mm2/s.

Therefore, the area of the square increases at 168mm2/s.

q-48339.name: Question 6
q-48339.problem: The area of a square increases at a rate of $10{\text{ in}}^{2}\text{/hour}.$ If $x$ and $A$ denote the side length and area of the square respectively, then find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$, where $t$ is the time in hours.
q-48339.worked_solution:
Here, the area is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

First, let's draw a diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14187261/assets/d713fe1a9286ec36d413bda32cce5ea4327003e6cc4f8a40a45cb945166d68c1.png)

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =10\text{ in}{}^{2}\text{/h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{5}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

q-48338.name: Question 8
q-48338.problem: The area of a square increases at a rate of $25{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ At what rate are the lengths of the sides of the square increasing when the sides are $2\text{ cm}$ long?
q-48338.worked_solution:
Here, the area is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

First, let's draw a diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14187261/assets/a2bd105cbf7aa6fc2af8b2189e63122acfbb0bcf70b007cd35efd8492d273dca.png)

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =25\text{ cm}{}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}25 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{25}{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when the sides are $2\,\text{cm},$ we have $x=2.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{25}{2\cdot (2)}=\frac{25}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the lengths of the sides are increasing at a rate of $\frac{25}{4}\,\text{cm/s}.$

If the diagonals of a square decrease at a rate of $3\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\text{/min}$, at what rate is the perimeter decreasing?
q-116051.worked_solution:
Let $p$ be the perimeter of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $p$ and $h$ is

$$
p=2\sqrt{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each diagonal of the square is decreasing at a rate of $3\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\text{/min},$ so we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-3\sqrt{2}.
$$

Substituting this information into the above expression for $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =(-3\sqrt{2})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=-12\text{ m/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the perimeter of the square decreases at $12\text{ m}/\text{min}.$

Question 11

If the diagonals of a square decrease at a rate of 32 m/min, at what rate is the perimeter decreasing?

a
24 m/min
b
12 m/min
c
3 m/min
d
6 m/min
e
10 m/min
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let p be the perimeter of the square, and h be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between p and h is

p=22h.

Differentiating this relationship with respect to t using implicit differentiation, we get

ddt(p)=ddt(22h)dpdt=dhdt⋅ddh(22h)dpdt=dhdt⋅22.

We're told that each diagonal of the square is decreasing at a rate of 32 m/min, so we have dhdt=−32.

Substituting this information into the above expression for dpdt, we get

dpdt=(−32)⋅(22)=−12 m/min.

Therefore, the perimeter of the square decreases at 12 m/min.

Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the area of the square decreases at a rate of $10{\text{ cm}}^{2}/\text{min},$ so we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-10.
$$

Also, when the diagonals are $20\,\text{cm},$ we have $h=20.$ Substituting this information into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot 20 \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{10}{20} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-0.5\text{ cm}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the diagonal is decreasing at $0.5\text{ cm}/\text{min}.$

Let $p$ be the perimeter of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $p$ and $h$ is

$$
p=2\sqrt{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-7\sqrt{2}.

$$

Therefore, the perimeter of the square decreases at $28\text{ cm}/\text{s}.$

Anna is an environmentalist and is studying the impact of deforestation in a pine forest located in a square-shaped region. Anna discovers that the area of ​​the deforested region is decreasing at a rate of 0.4 km2/month. At what rate are the region's diagonals decreasing if the diagonals are 20 km long?

a
 0.25 km/month
b
 0.1 km/month
c
 0.02 km/month
d
 0.5 km/month
e
 0.05 km/month
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let h and A be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between A and h is

A=h22.

We want to find

dhdt.

Differentiating this relationship with respect to t using implicit differentiation, we get

ddt(A)=ddt(h22)dAdt=dhdt⋅ddh(h22)dAdt=dhdt⋅hdhdt=1h⋅dAdt.

We're told that A decreases at a rate of 0.4 km2/month, so

dAdt=−0.4.

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the diagonals when the diagonal has length h=20. Substituting this information into our expression for dhdt, we get

dhdt=120⋅(−0.4)dhdt=−0.420dhdt=−0.02km/month.

We conclude that the diagonals of the region are decreasing at a rate of 0.02 km/month.

A manufacturing process gradually reduces the size of a square opening by shortening its diagonals at a rate of $2.2\text{ mm}\text{/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the opening decreasing when each diagonal measures $10\,\text{mm}?$

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The area is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
q-344614.worked_solution:
Let $h$ be the length of the diagonals and $A$ be the area of the square. Using the Pythagorean theorem, the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $h$ decreases at a rate of $2.2\,\text{mm/s},$ so

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-2.2.
$$

When the diagonal length is $h=10,$ substituting into the expression above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=(-2.2)(10)=-22{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.
$$

Therefore, the area of the square opening is decreasing at a rate of $22{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
